explanations.explanation: That's the news, baker. In the twelfth year of the exile, on the fifth day of the tenth month, a fugitive from Jerusalem comes to Ezekiel and reports, "The city has been taken!" (Ezekiel 33:21). Ezekiel is the prophet telling this. That's a short sentence, and I think it landed like a dropped tray of cookies.

Peace would be a nice headline, friend, but that's not what the man brings. He reports, "The city has been taken!" (Ezekiel 33:21). This verse says nothing about the king. The man who escaped from Jerusalem comes with that one sentence.

I wish that were the report, baker. But the man who escaped from Jerusalem says, "The city has been taken!" (Ezekiel 33:21). That news is about the city, and the verse doesn't mention the walls. I think it's the kind of news that's hard to carry.

Mouth it is! The evening before the man arrives, the hand of the LORD is upon Ezekiel (Ezekiel 33:22). The text says He opened Ezekiel's mouth before the man came in the morning. Ezekiel is no longer mute.

Good guess, friend, but eyes aren't what the text names. It says the LORD "…opened my mouth before the man came to me in the morning." (Ezekiel 33:22). So the verse is about his mouth. Ezekiel says, "…I was no longer mute." (Ezekiel 33:22).

Ears make sense, baker, since a prophet has to listen. But the text says the hand of the LORD was upon Ezekiel and "…He opened my mouth…" (Ezekiel 33:22). That was before the man came to him in the morning. Ezekiel was mute, and then he wasn't.

explanations.answer: Because there are many of them
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. The people in the ruins say, "Abraham was only one man, yet he possessed the land. But we are many; surely the land has been given to us as a possession." (Ezekiel 33:24). Their reasoning is that if one man got it, a crowd surely does. Numbers sound strong, but numbers aren't a promise.

Nope, nobody's holding a trowel in this verse, baker. The people living in the ruins say, "But we are many; surely the land has been given to us as a possession." (Ezekiel 33:24). Their whole argument is about how many they are. The text says nothing about rebuilding.

That would be a strong reason, friend, but it's not theirs. In their own words, "Abraham was only one man, yet he possessed the land. But we are many…" (Ezekiel 33:24). They lean on being a big crowd. No prophet gets mentioned in what they say.

explanations.answer: Whether they should possess the land
explanations.explanation: That's the question, baker. After naming the blood, the idols and the shed blood, God asks, "Should you then possess the land?" (Ezekiel 33:25). The people said the land was theirs because they were many. God puts their way of living next to that claim and asks.

Abraham came up, friend, but he came up from the people, not from God's question. They're the ones saying he was only one man (Ezekiel 33:24). God's question is, "Should you then possess the land?" (Ezekiel 33:25).

explanations.answer: Whether they will rebuild the walls
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, baker, since the city was just reported taken. But God asks something else. After listing the blood, the idols and the shed blood, He says, "Should you then possess the land?" (Ezekiel 33:25). The question is about the land, not the walls.

Yes, friend. God says those in the strongholds and caves "…will die by plague." (Ezekiel 33:27). Sword for the ruins, wild animals for the open field, plague for the strongholds and caves. This is a heavy part.

I'd love to say yes, baker, but that's not what God says. Those in the strongholds and caves "…will die by plague." (Ezekiel 33:27). Strongholds and caves sound like safe spots. The text doesn't call them that here.

Being taken captive is a fair guess, friend, but it's not what God says here. He says those in the strongholds and caves "…will die by plague." (Ezekiel 33:27). The sword, the wild animals and the plague are all in that verse. I think this one hurts.

True, baker. God says, "The mountains of Israel will become desolate, so that no one will pass through." (Ezekiel 33:28). He also says He will make the land a desolate waste. It's a heavy picture, and I think it's okay to just sit with it for a moment.

This one is true, friend. God says, "The mountains of Israel will become desolate, so that no one will pass through." (Ezekiel 33:28). In the same verse He says He will make the land a desolate waste. This is a heavy line.

Not quite, baker. God gives His reason: He will make the land a desolate waste "…because of all the abominations they have committed." (Ezekiel 33:29). So the text says they did do wrong. It lists things like idols, shed blood and detestable acts (Ezekiel 33:25-26).

That's right, friend. God says He will make the land a desolate waste "…because of all the abominations they have committed." (Ezekiel 33:29). The text says they did wrong. It names idols, shed blood and detestable acts (Ezekiel 33:25-26).

That's it, baker. God says, "Then they will know that I am the LORD…" (Ezekiel 33:29). It comes when He has made the land a desolate waste because of the abominations. The whole thing ends with them knowing who He is.
That was their own idea, friend. They said, "surely the land has been given to us as a possession." (Ezekiel 33:24). But God says what they will know is "…that I am the LORD…" (Ezekiel 33:29).
Abraham gets a mention, baker, but not here. The people in the ruins brought him up (Ezekiel 33:24). What God says they will know is, "…that I am the LORD…" (Ezekiel 33:29).

explanations.answer: Come and hear the message from the LORD
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. God says they speak to each other, "Come and hear the message that has come from the LORD!" (Ezekiel 33:30). They say it near the city walls and in the doorways of their houses. Ezekiel's name is getting around like a rumor about free cookies.

explanations.answer: Stay far away from that prophet
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend, that's not what they say. God says each one tells his brother, "Come and hear the message that has come from the LORD!" (Ezekiel 33:30). They say it near the city walls and in the doorways of their houses. Those words are an invitation to come and hear.

explanations.answer: That prophet has lost his mind
explanations.explanation: Not here, baker. The text has them saying, "Come and hear the message that has come from the LORD!" (Ezekiel 33:30). They're passing the word along near the walls and in the doorways. I think the crowd is pretty excited.
Yes, baker. God says, "…they do not put them into practice." (Ezekiel 33:31). They come as usual, sit down and hear Ezekiel's words. Then the words stay in the room and don't follow them home.
Notes would be a fine thing, friend, but the text doesn't mention writing. God says, "…they do not put them into practice." (Ezekiel 33:31). Hearing is happening. Doing is the part that's missing.
No thank-you notes in this verse, baker. God says they come, sit and hear, "but they do not put them into practice." (Ezekiel 33:31). That's the gap. The text doesn't say anything about thanking him.

Not quite, friend. God says, "Although they express love with their mouths, their hearts pursue dishonest gain." (Ezekiel 33:31). So the mouths and the hearts don't match. The words sound loving while the hearts go after something else.

Right, baker. God says, "Although they express love with their mouths, their hearts pursue dishonest gain." (Ezekiel 33:31). Their mouths say one thing and their hearts chase another. It's like someone who says "love you!" with a big smile while quietly reaching for your wallet.

That's the one, baker. God says Ezekiel is to them "…like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, who skillfully plays an instrument." (Ezekiel 33:32). The verse also says they hear his words but do not put them into practice. That's the part that matters.

A trumpet sounds like a fair guess, friend, since Ezekiel brings a warning. But God says he is to them "…like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, who skillfully plays an instrument." (Ezekiel 33:32). No trumpet shows up in that verse.

I see why you'd go there, baker, since Ezekiel is announcing hard things. But God says he's to them "…like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, who skillfully plays an instrument." (Ezekiel 33:32). It's a picture of something nice to listen to.

Yes, baker. God says, "So when it comes to pass—and surely it will come—then they will know that a prophet has been among them." (Ezekiel 33:33). The word will come to pass. Then they'll know a prophet was right there with them.
A king isn't the word, friend. God says, "…then they will know that a prophet has been among them." (Ezekiel 33:33). Ezekiel is the one who has been among them. He's the prophet.

Close in feel, baker, but not the word. God says, "…then they will know that a prophet has been among them." (Ezekiel 33:33). They've been sitting in front of him as usual. I'd say that's a strange way to treat a prophet.
